chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.citation: Shin, C et al. (2021). Anaerobic membrane bioreactor model for design and prediction of domestic wastewater treatment process performance. CHEM ENG J.
chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.citation: Sher, F et al. (2020). Implications of advanced wastewater treatment: Electrocoagulation and electroflocculation of effluent discharged from a wastewater treatment plant. J WATER PROCESS ENG.
chunks.text: This study deals with wastewater treatment on a pilot-scale plant set up by electrochemical technology. The electrocoagulation and electroflocculation techniques were applied with a revived design to meet the needs of the process to remove suspended solids and micropollutants out of the wastewater stream. By using various settings of applied currents, the process was tested for the better quality of effluent using water from the outflow of primary sedimentation tank and treated water from the outflow of secondary sedimentation tank. Furthermore, the results are optimized for a better downstream separation process. Wastewater from primary sedimentation tank was treated with both Fe and Al electrodes. In the case of Fe electrodes, more than 50 % of COD removal was observed which was about 12-18 % with Al electrodes. The coagulation dose of Fe and Al electrodes were measured, on the basis of AFS produced and according to Faraday's Law. With both Fe and Al electrodes, the coagulation dose went on increasing with increasing current density.

chunks.citation: Jasper, JT et al. (2017). Toxic Byproduct Formation during Electrochemical Treatment of Latrine Wastewater. ENVIRON SCI TECHNOL.
chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.text: The facility discussed in this study is a large coastal WRRF with the average peak influent flow of 5.30 × 10 5 m 3 d − 1 (140 MGD) located in California. The facility is equipped with chemically enhanced primary treatment (CEPT) that utilizes ferric chloride and anionic polymers. On average, approximately 20 % of their primary effluent is sent to the facility's two trickling filters equipped with one clarifier each (outside the scope of this research) and the remainder 80 % is treated at the facility's activated sludge units. Most of the facility effluent is used for groundwater recharge and to feed a hydraulic barrier to prevent seawater intrusion. The remainder is discharged into the Pacific Ocean. Since the secondary effluent quality needs to be suitable with the subsequent water reuse operations, effective removal of TSS and BOD is paramount. In the last two decades, this facility underwent modifications in its activated sludge units' configuration. These included an upgrade from conventional carbon oxidation to nitrogen removal, implemented to improve secondary solids separation and to improve energy-efficiency [10] .

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .

chunks.citation: Du, R et al. (2019). Partial denitrification providing nitrite: Opportunities of extending application for anammox. ENVIRON INT.
chunks.text: The nitritation is a common attempt for generating NO 2 − -N for anammox bacteria. This process consists of two pivots: enrichment of AOB and suppression of nitrite oxidizing bacteria (NOB) by making selective pressure on the two groups of bacteria (Fig. 1 ). The primary strategies for controlling nitritation include low dissolved oxygen (DO) (Laureni et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013) , high temperature, short sludge retention time (SRT) (Kouba et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Pollice et al., 2002) , real-time aeration control (Gu et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2007) , as well as the free ammonia (FA) and free nitrous acid (FNA) based sludge treatment (Wang et al., 2016) . However, there are still major issues in the practical application for both of the high-strength wastewater and mainstream treatment.
